nodes.question: What kind of indicators does the social pillar of the three-pillar model include?
nodes.answer: The social pillar includes community-based considerations, such as indicators related to education and access to decent livelihood.
nodes.paragraph: 2019). This framing of sustainability is sometimes referred to as triple- bottom line, or people, planet, profit (Purvis et al. 2019 ). The three-pillar model has also been described as economically dominant (James and Magee 2016) and anthropocentric (Purvis et al. 2019). This three-pillar approach may there- fore be an inappropriate conceptual framework for viewing agricultural sustainability as it has a foundation in business and therefore different ontological perspectives (Purvis et al. 2019). There is likely contention regarding definitions within these three pillars. However, for the purpose of this review, is can be broadly described where the environmental pil- lar incorporates indicators for the physical environment for example, indicators relating to greenhouse gas emissions or eutrophication of waterways; the social pillar incorporates community-based considerations for example, indicators relating to education and access to decent livelihood; the economic pillar incorporates classical fiscal indicators, for example, return on investment and profitability. A literature review conducted by Chopin et al. (2021) explored on-farm sustainability assessment tools and con- cluded a wider framing is required when undertaking agri- cultural sustainability measurements due to emergent rea- sons including resilience and stability.

nodes.question: How does money contribute to social relationships according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Money contributes to social relationships by playing a role in communication and the creation of social bonds or signs of belonging to a society.
nodes.paragraph: Beyond its three func- tions as defined by Aristotle namely the role of medium of exchange, store of value and unit of account money might play a role in communication and in the creation of social bonds or signs of belonging to a society. nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What alternative term reflects the social objective of certain currencies?
nodes.answer: The term "social currencies" reflects the social objective of certain currencies.
nodes.paragraph: Thus, as J r me Blanc notes, we may come across the term "complemen- tary currencies" which reflects the fact that these types of currencies exist alongside national money (or fiat money), whereas their economic and social interests for a community are expressed through the term "community currencies". The emphasis is placed on their social objective by speaking of "social currencies", and some monetary systems can also be Sustainability Science described as "citizen currencies" to underline the fact that they are the result of a formal citizen involvement. Finally, as Blanc notes, the term "alternative" is not new, since several authors were already using it in the mid-2000s to charac- terise several specific economic arrangements (North 2006, 2007; Maurer 2005; Leyshon et al. 2003). Therefore, we use the term alternative currencies because we believe it defines the idea of offering alternatives to national or multinational currency systems, while de facto encompassing the existing specificities. However, in English, the term CCS which stands for complementary currency system is also used to describe a specific unit (or system) of account that complements the official currency and has been developed by a group of agents (individuals, economic and social structures, local authorities or banks) that has formed a local network with a view to accounting for and regulating exchanges of goods and services.

nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What gap in knowledge does this study aim to fill?
nodes.answer: This study aims to fill the gap regarding public preferences for the principles of a wellbeing economy as countries recover from the disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
nodes.paragraph: Similarly to those proposed by WEAII and Measuring What Matters, these indicators are cross-sectoral in that they include indicators commonly reported on by dif- ferent government departments (for example, health, treas- ury, education, labour and environment). While these indi- cators can all be considered important within an individual department and fall within their remit, some of our most intractable societal problems are cross-sectional in nature. These problems are likely to require cooperation across mul- tiple stakeholders to solve. Whilst the principles of a wellbe- ing economy are increasingly being embraced by policymak - ers, to our knowledge no study to date has sought to identify the preferences of the general public for the principles of a wellbeing economy as countries re-build following the dis- ruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. This study aimed to fill this gap in our current knowledge by assessing the relative importance to the Australian gen- eral public of the key principles of a wellbeing economy and to investigate the potential for heterogeneity in preferences in relation to these key principles between demographic subgroups. 2 Methods 2.1 Survey An online survey was developed and delivered to a sample of Australian adults (aged 18 years and above).
